AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups

Pure — best for anonymous hookups

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

“I wouldn’t let more than a few days go by before transitioning to an in-person meeting or at least a video call,” Suzannah Weiss, sex/couples therapist and resident sexologist for Erojoy, tells Mashable.

Hinge is my pick for the best dating app for people over 40 who want a relationship and a little more to go on than someone’s best vacation photo. You can like a specific photo or prompt answer and attach a comment, giving you a way to start a conversation about something you noticed. Matching and chatting are free, though you’re limited in how many likes you can send each day.

Your questionable karaoke choices, the hobby you’ve taken up, or what makes a weekend feel well spent can all give someone a reason to reach out. If you’re returning to dating after a long relationship, prompts help you decide what to share without having to explain your entire life story.

I picked Hinge because its profile format gives you something useful to work with before you match. A thoughtful answer can reveal a shared interest, a difference in priorities, or an easy opening question.

“Comment on something in the person’s profile, like an activity they’re doing in their photos or an interest listed in their bio,” Weiss tells Mashable. “This will make your message stand out amid the generic ones.”

If writing about yourself feels awkward, Hinge’s “Your World” prompts, developed with psychotherapist Esther Perel, offer prompts like “I’m in my element when…” and “I could stay up all night talking about…”

"Match Note" is a useful feature for sharing more personal information you want potential matches to know without putting it on your public profile. You might use it to explain that you’re sober, recently out of a relationship, or looking for non-monogamy. The note is shared when there’s mutual interest, and the other person has to acknowledge it before moving forward. (So they can't later say, "I didn't know.")

For opening-message nerves, Hinge's optional "Convo Starters" suggests topics based on someone’s photos and prompt answers. You still write the opener, with a few ideas to help you get started.

Hinge also has a “Hidden Words” feature that lets you filter unwanted words, phrases, and emoji in comments attached to incoming likes. Verification requirements vary by region, with biometric Face Check required in some locations.

Match is worth a look if you’re over 40, want a relationship, and like having enough profile detail to work out whether someone interests you. It’s my pick for detailed profiles, particularly if you want to explain your hobbies, family life, and relationship goals in more detail.

It also has a history of reaching older daters. In the 2026 SSRS survey, 33 percent of U.S. adults aged 50 and older who had ever used a dating site or app said they’d tried Match. That put it second among the platforms listed for that age group.

If you’re returning to dating after divorce or losing a partner, the profile format gives you space to explain what you’re looking for now. Maybe you want to remarry, find a regular travel companion, or meet someone who understands that your custody schedule determines which weekends you’re free.

I picked Match because its profiles let you picture how someone might fit into your life. Interests, lifestyle details, and relationship preferences provide useful starting points when you’re deciding who you’d like to meet.

Erica Arrechea, founder and CEO of Cinqe Matchmaking, describes the practical questions that can shape later-life dating: “Do we live together? Do we get married? Do we travel together but keep separate homes? How involved are our children? Where do we spend holidays?"

Those are the kinds of considerations I’d keep in mind while browsing. A shared love of travel is a conversation starter; finding out whether your schedules and expectations line up helps you decide where that conversation might go.

You can browse profiles before subscribing, and mutual matches can message each other for free. That makes it easier to get a feel for the people nearby before deciding whether a paid plan is worth your money.

Match’s reporting tools let you flag concerns from a profile or message, including harassment, requests for money, and inappropriate behavior during an in-person date. Reports are anonymous.

Its subscription history also deserves a mention. In August 2025, Match Group agreed to a $14 million FTC settlement over allegations involving misleading subscription guarantees, account restrictions after unsuccessful billing disputes, and difficult cancellation processes. The agreement required clearer disclosures and simpler cancellation mechanisms — relevant context if you’re considering a paid plan.

Read our full review of AdultFriendFinder.

Bumble is worth trying if you’re over 40, looking for a relationship, and ready to see someone other than the same three people in your Hinge feed. Profile prompts and dating intentions give you a starting point, and you can match and chat without paying for a subscription.

If you’ve lost track of who’s allowed to message first, fair. Bumble introduced "Opening Moves," which let men respond to a woman’s prompt, then removed the feature in Australia and Mexico. In August 2026, it made a broader change: Either person can now send the first message. You get one opener, and the conversation stays locked until the recipient replies. They have 72 hours to respond.

That takes some pressure off women who are tired of thinking up every opening line, while keeping the other person in control of whether the chat continues. If you’re juggling work, family commitments, or a calendar booked three weekends out, the longer reply window is welcome breathing room.

I picked Bumble because it has useful tools for fitting dating around the rest of your life. "Snooze Mode" is one of my favorites: You can pause your visibility to new people for a day, a week, or indefinitely while keeping your existing conversations. When you need a break, your profile can wait until you’re ready to pick things up again.

If getting your profile together is the part you’re dreading, Bumble’s AI Profile Guidance and AI Photo Feedback offer suggestions on your bio and photos. Profile Guidance launched globally, while Photo Feedback initially launched in the U.S. A little help may be welcome when you’ve rewritten “a typical Sunday” so many times you’ve forgotten what you do on Sundays.

Bumble also has practical tools for meeting someone new. ID Verification checks your government-issued ID and a live selfie, while "Share Date" lets you send a trusted contact your match’s name and photo, plus when and where you’re meeting. It makes the “here’s who I’m going out with” text easier to put together.

There’s one issue I’m still hung up on. In 2025, users reported seeing people they’d already blocked, prompting founder Whitney Wolfe Herd to publicly promise improvements to trust and safety. That history still factors into my recommendation.

OkCupid is my pick for values-driven matches, especially if you’re over 40 and know which differences you can happily live with — and which ones would turn dinner into a debate you’ve already had too many times. Its matching questions give you a way to compare views on politics, relationships, and everyday habits before starting a conversation.

It’s also worth considering if mainstream profile options have left you feeling boxed in. OkCupid offers over 60 ways to identify across gender and orientation and lets you specify what kind of relationship you want. Whether you’re looking for monogamy, exploring non-monogamy, or dating without a wedding deadline, you can put those intentions on your profile.

I picked OkCupid because its questions give you something specific to consider as you browse. You answer questions about yourself and what you’d accept in a partner, and those responses help shape your match percentages. You can spend time on the subjects you care about, whether that’s religion, political beliefs, or how someone approaches a relationship.

That format works well when you have an established life and want to share it with someone whose priorities match yours. A funny bio might get your attention, but someone’s answers can give you a specific question to ask — or a shared opinion to bond over. Since the free version lets you browse, match, and chat, you can take that curiosity into a conversation without paying for a subscription.

Tinder is my pick for casual dating over 40, whether you’re easing back into the scene after a long relationship or enjoying being single and seeing where things go. You can keep your profile straightforward, browse nearby people, and chat with mutual matches for free.

It’s also a place to be direct about what you want. The "Relationship Goals" feature lets you display the kind of connection you’re looking for, so “something casual” doesn’t have to become an awkward reveal three conversations in. If your plans are flexible, you can say that, too.

I picked Tinder because getting started doesn’t require a lengthy questionnaire. You both swipe right, you match, and either person can message first.

The experience still depends on your local crowd. In this r/datingoverforty discussion, recommendations vary by location, and people describe different levels of success across the same apps. Tinder is worth comparing with your other options, particularly if you keep seeing the same faces elsewhere.

Your bio gives someone a reason to choose you out of that swipe deck. Mention the concert you’re excited for or your strong opinions about the best breakfast spot in town. Give a potential match an easier opening than “So, what brings you here?”

If you’d feel more comfortable bringing friends along, Tinder’s Group Hangouts let you turn meeting new people into a group outing. One person picks an activity (like karaoke) and invites at least two friends. Once your group has three members, you can browse other groups, match, and chat about getting together. Everyone needs their own Tinder profile, and the feature is available in the U.S. and select markets.

Tinder has also expanded "Face Check," its video-selfie verification process. The scan checks that you’re a live person, compares your face with your profile photos, and looks for the same face across multiple accounts. It involves biometric data: Tinder says it deletes the video after review and retains encrypted facial data for verification and duplicate-account detection. That’s worth knowing before you sign up.

eharmony is for the over-40 dater who wants a long-term relationship and has the patience for a thorough sign-up process. When I tested it, the questionnaire asked about everything from why I wanted a relationship to whether I’d prefer sharing a bed or sleeping in separate bedrooms. If you like thinking through those details before browsing, there’s plenty to consider here.

You’ll also need a budget. The free experience left me scrolling through blurred photos and encountering frequent subscription prompts, which made it difficult to get excited about the people I might meet.

I picked eharmony for its detailed approach to compatibility, though it wouldn’t be my first recommendation for everyone. The questionnaire explores relationship expectations, everyday habits, and how you react when someone upsets you. Some questions gave me useful things to think about; others had me wondering how much longer I’d be sitting there choosing between pictures of shapes.

I entered details about my work, education, children, and marital status, then answered prompts and wrote a bio. If you’re dating after divorce or losing a partner, those profile details can help explain your circumstances without having to repeat the basics in every conversation.

What frustrated me was getting through all that and still being unable to see my featured matches’ photos without paying. My first suggested profile was two and a half hours away, and the other two were also over an hour away. That was my experience in a small Virginia town, but it’s a useful reminder to check the recommendations you receive before committing to a subscription.

I also found the upgrade process pushy. A “Welcome Gift” turned out to be a subscription discount, and clicking through took me to a payment screen. I could back out and continue with the free version, but the experience made paying feel like the expected next step.

For someone who wants detailed compatibility information and is comfortable paying to use the service, eharmony may earn a spot on the shortlist. My own experience puts it behind Hinge and Match: I wanted to spend more time getting to know potential dates and less time getting through sign-up and subscription screens.

Hinge is my pick for the best dating app for people over 40, particularly if you want a relationship and prefer getting a sense of someone’s personality before matching. You can like or comment on a specific photo or prompt, giving you a more natural conversation starter than a generic “hey.”

It isn’t the only option worth trying. Match is worth comparing if you want more detailed profiles, while Tinder is an option for casual dating. Start with the free experience, see who’s nearby, and then decide whether to commit to a subscription.

Yes. Hinge is my top recommendation: You can send a limited number of likes, attach comments, and chat with mutual matches without subscribing. Paid plans add benefits, but you don’t need one to have a conversation.

OkCupid, Bumble, and Tinder are other options to compare. When choosing a free dating app, look beyond “free to sign up” and check whether you can match and message without paying.

There’s no universal answer. Your experience depends on where you live, who you want to meet, and how dating fits around your existing commitments. Being over 40 doesn’t automatically mean you’re more confident, looking for marriage, or interested only in people with the same relationship history. Instead of choosing an app based on age alone, think about the life you want to share.

I’d start with Tinder if you’re exploring casual dating and Bumble if you want an alternative with more structure around opening conversations. Neither is automatically better because you’re over 40, and I wouldn’t choose Bumble solely for its old “women message first” reputation.

Try the free versions and compare the people you see within your preferred age range and distance. Daters in the r/datingoverforty community report different experiences depending on their location, so someone else’s favorite may not be your best local option.

Use recent photos, say what kind of connection you want, and give someone a glimpse of what spending time with you would look like. Specific details — your Sunday hiking routine, love of terrible horror movies, or search for a regular doubles partner — give people more to respond to than “I enjoy having fun.”

You don’t need to write a résumé or disclose your relationship history. Mention the priorities that affect compatibility, like having children or wanting a relationship without living together.

“Make sure to select recent photos as it can be misleading to use photos of you when you were younger,” Weiss tells Mashable.

Protect your personal information, meet somewhere public, and let a trusted friend know your plans. A video call can help you get a better sense of someone before meeting.

“Meet in a public place, as usual, and have a friend check in with you later in the night or the next morning to make sure you’re OK,” Weiss advises.

Never send money or gifts to an online love interest you haven’t met in person. If you suspect a scam, stop communicating, report the account, and talk to someone you trust.

Pay attention to patterns of pressure, inconsistency, and financial requests — not just an awkward bio or a bad profile photo.

Requests for money for travel, medical bills, or another supposed emergency.

Offers to teach you how to invest, particularly in cryptocurrency.

Repeated excuses for why they can’t meet.

Profile photos that appear under another name in a reverse-image search.

Pressure to move off the app immediately or disregard your boundaries is also a reason to slow down. “Steer away from anything that requests payment or asks you to move to another platform right away,” Weiss says.

I wouldn’t make an exclusive app your first stop simply because you’re an established professional. An application process or selective membership doesn’t tell you whether someone shares your goals — or whether there will be enough people nearby you want to meet.

For this guide, I’m prioritizing apps I can recommend on their everyday usefulness: profiles, messaging access, preferences, and the experience of finding potential dates. I’d try those before treating exclusivity as a reason to sign up.

Choosing a dating app shouldn’t require downloading six of them and paying for three subscriptions. I’ve spent years testing dating apps for Mashable, and this guide draws on that hands-on experience, expert commentary, and feedback from daters over 40. Here’s what goes into my recommendations:

Hands-on testing: I create profiles, browse potential matches, and use the messaging tools to see how each app works. I try the free experience and evaluate paid upgrades, paying particular attention to what you can do without subscribing. Free registration doesn’t mean much if you can’t see profiles or have a conversation.

Relevance to dating over 40: I look at how well each app lets you communicate your relationship goals, interests, and everyday priorities, including children, lifestyle preferences, and plans for the future. I also consider whether useful filters are available for free or locked behind a subscription. An app doesn’t earn a place here just because it markets itself to “mature singles.”

Expert and community perspectives: I consult relationship professionals who aren’t affiliated with dating apps and read Reddit discussions and app-store reviews for perspectives beyond my own. Feedback from people dating in their 40s and beyond helps identify recurring frustrations, but I don’t treat an individual success story (or a terrible date) as proof of what everyone will experience.

Ongoing reassessment: I revisit recommendations as features, messaging rules, subscription benefits, and ownership change. If an app changes substantially, its previous review isn’t enough to justify keeping it on the list.

Tabitha Britt is an award-winning freelance journalist, editor, and SEO/AEO strategist. Aside from reviewing dating apps and sex toys for Mashable, Tabitha is also the founding editor-in-chief of DO YOU ENDO — a digital magazine by individuals with endometriosis, for individuals with endometriosis. She has a Master's degree in Creative Publishing and Critical Journalism from The New School for Social Research and is a grad of Sextech School. You can find more of her work in various online publications, including National Geographic, Glamour, Better Homes & Gardens, and Everyday Health.

#326. The FDA wants to pull its approval of a drug. It’s not so easy.

The regulator says Tavneos was approved on the basis of manipulated study data. Should patients still have access to it?

In May 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration released a lengthy briefing document on an experimental medication for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis that often damages the kidneys and lungs. The agency was on the fence about whether to approve the treatment, and it wanted an independent advisory committee to weigh in. Among the questions at hand: Was the drug meaningfully better than existing therapies?

Participants in the study, which had been conducted by the California biotechnology company ChemoCentryx, did appear to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year. But according to the FDA, it was hard to interpret the results because the study’s design had been less than optimal. Some advisory committee members expressed a similar view. The effect of the drug, said one, “is just not well verified by this study.”

At the same time, many patients, and some physicians, saw in the data a potentially helpful medication, one that might lessen patients’ reliance on steroids, which are highly effective but often cause severe side effects.

The advisory committee ultimately voted narrowly to recommend approval, and the FDA followed that advice, greenlighting the drug on October 7, 2021. The drug, marketed as Tavneos, started making its way into clinics. A year after approval, ChemoCentryx was acquired by Amgen, one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies. The cost, even today, isn’t minor: $220,000 per year, according to Drugs.com. In fiscal year 2025, sales of Tavneos reached nearly half a billion dollars.

This financial windfall has unfolded despite a long-roiling investor lawsuit—one that incidentally uncovered what the FDA today believes is evidence that ChemoCentryx employees manipulated the data in the pivotal trial submitted to the agency. In April of this year, the FDA issued a letter proposing that Tavneos be withdrawn from the US market, citing reports of serious, sometimes fatal, liver injury, and arguing that the drug now lacks “substantial evidence” that it works.

These revelations have triggered a dramatic cascade of events. This summer, the New England Journal of Medicine retracted a paper describing the clinical trial and Tavneos was taken off the market in the European Union. The United Kingdom has announced that it, too, will remove the product from the market. And on October 29, a court hearing is expected to proceed over Zoom to consider a proposed $69 million settlement for the lawsuit.

But the fate of Tavneos, at least in the United States, is far from sealed. Amgen has pushed back against its critics, insisting that—whatever the details of ChemoCentryx’s data handling—its drug works as advertised and should stay on the market. In July, the company submitted a 104-page document to the FDA stating that “the totality of the evidence supports the continued availability of TAVNEOS.”

Some patients and academic experts also believe the drug is an important treatment option. “This appears to be an efficacious medication,” said Eric Roberts, an epidemiologist at the University of California, San Francisco, who co-authored an independent registry study of Tavneos.

The dispute is emblematic of the FDA’s longstanding struggle to regulate drugs of uncertain efficacy, said Reshma Ramachandran, a physician and co-director of the Yale Collaboration for Regulatory Rigor, Integrity, and Transparency. Absent more rigorous studies, either before or after a drug goes on the market, Ramachandran worries, “we’re just going to be living in uncertainty in terms of whether or not these drugs actually work.”

For American consumers, the saga of Tavneos also raises potent questions around the safeguards in place to ensure the integrity of drug approvals, particularly when a relatively small company conducts the pivotal trial and has so much riding on the success of a single drug.

Chloe Cusano was a 20-year-old college student when she was struck, this past December, with unbearable pain in her legs, as well as bouts of breathlessness from routine tasks like walking upstairs or bending down to retrieve her dog’s water dish. After going to the emergency room, she was hospitalized for more than two weeks, during which she was diagnosed with ANCA-associated vasculitis, or AAV, an umbrella term for a group of rare diseases in which the immune system mistakenly attacks its own blood vessels. When it was first identified, the condition was usually fatal.

Over the past four decades, scientists have developed drugs that allow many AAV patients to live a relatively normal lifespan. Because the disease can rapidly lead to organ failure, particularly of the kidneys and lungs, patients are immediately started on a high dose of steroids to rapidly tamp down inflammation. They also typically receive slower-acting medications that target the underlying disease process.

Steroids, however, have severe side effects. Within a month and a half of going on the steroids, Cusano recalled, she gained 40 pounds. Her emotions were “just like crazy,” swinging from intense sadness to anger. She had trouble falling asleep, and when she did fall asleep, she was haunted by another side effect: nightmares. “I did not like it at all,” she recalls.

AAV patients may need to take steroids for months to years, and Tavneos was supposed to replace or reduce their use.

David Pisetsky, a rheumatologist and researcher at the Duke University School of Medicine, was on the FDA advisory committee that considered the ChemoCentryx trial data. He voted against recommending approval, in part because many patients in the control group received just one round of a slower-acting medication — rituximab — in addition to steroids when, in the real world, they would have received two, according to Pisetsky. The trial’s design, he said, made the results difficult to interpret.

In an editorial in the journal Rheumatology, Mike Putman, medical director of the Vasculitis Program at the Medical College of Wisconsin, and co-authors would later make a similar case: Patients in the comparison group did not receive treatment consistent with the current standard of care. “It is somewhat debate-able about what the ‘standard of care’ would have been” when the study was done, Putman wrote in an email to Undark. “We had not yet established rituximab as maintenance therapy at that point, though most people were already doing that.”

Other members of the advisory committee were persuaded, including Walter Kraft, a clinical pharmacologist and researcher at Thomas Jefferson University. He voted yes to approval. “I felt the evidence, though limited, met the societal and therapeutic goals,” he said during the meeting. Requiring another trial, he added, could delay the drug’s approval by several years.

But that vote, he told Undark in a recent interview, was “based upon an assumption that the sponsor was following the rules of the road.”

These days, a significant number of drugs approved by the FDA start out at a small company with few or no medications on the market, said Sean Nicholson, an economist at Cornell University. Large companies increasingly recognize that their comparative advantage is not in developing breakthrough science, which is more likely to come from “nimble, small startup biotechs,” so rather than trying to compete, Nicholson said, a big company will look to buy or partner with the smaller company.

That’s what happened with ChemoCentryx, which was bought by Amgen for nearly $4 billion one year after the FDA issued its approval of Tavneos.

When bringing a drug to market, small companies face a slightly different set of incentives from large companies, said David Ridley, a health economist at the Duke University Fuqua School of Business. A large company with many products in its pipeline may more readily abandon an experimental drug rather than invest in costly late-stage testing. “Small companies have more to lose,” he wrote in an email to Undark. “The entire company can be at stake. That urgency can drive them to work harder and move faster.”

“In rare cases,” he added, “they might cut corners.”

Back in May 2021, Tavneos’ approval appeared far from certain. Almost immediately after the FDA released its briefing document for the advisory committee meeting, ChemoCentryx’s stock value plummeted, and its shareholders sued for securities fraud.

Four years later, as part of that lawsuit, a report was filed, alleging that ChemoCentryx had not, in fact, followed the rules of the road. The report indicated that the company’s own trial analysis originally found that the patients receiving Tavneos had not achieved better one-year remission rates than the patients who received the usual treatment.

After company employees unblinded the trial data—meaning they looked to see which study participants had actually received the drug and which had received a placebo—they selected a handful of patients whose remission status would be reassessed. This readjudication, as it is called by the FDA, violated the study’s protocol. What’s more, the agency alleges, the patients were cherry-picked to get the results the company needed for approval.

ChemoCentryx did not disclose the original results, nor the fact that it had reassessed the original data, to the FDA.

In December 2025, Tracy Beth Høeg became acting director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, or CDER.

In an email to Undark, Høeg noted that legally, she can’t speak to the specifics of how this issue came to her attention. But, she noted, “One of my key roles as CDER acting director was letting everyone know my door was open, and I encouraged CDER employees to speak openly with me, especially about matters potentially affecting public safety.”

“When I learned of this case,” she continued, “I distinctly remember thinking this story had so much intrigue that it could easily be made into a movie.”

But the repercussions, Høeg argued with unusual candor, are very real. “Essentially ChemoCentryx swindled billions of dollars by developing a drug that gained FDA approval only because they manipulated the data,” she wrote. Since the drug went onto the market, it has been linked to eight deaths and dozens of hospitalizations. “This can be a deadly drug,” wrote Høeg, “and we don’t know if it works.”

Such was the essence of the FDA’s letter sent in April to Amgen, in which the agency proposed to withdraw approval of Tavneos. The retraction of the Tavneos trial data by the New England Journal of Medicine followed two months later, at the request of the study’s two academic authors.

“This will be a pivotal moment for rheumatology,” wrote Putman, in a lengthy essay on Substack. It’s a story not just about Tavneos, he argued, but evidence that the normal systems of scientific oversight — including peer review and regulatory approval — “failed to detect a shocking case” of alleged data manipulation.

According to Amgen, ChemoCentryx’s actions were less than ideal, but they don’t amount to data manipulation—and they certainly don’t warrant withdrawal of Tavneos.

In the 104-page document submitted to the FDA this summer, Amgen said that ChemoCentryx’s re-adjudication doesn’t “align with the approach Amgen would have taken.” Amgen called it “unfortunate” that ChemoCentryx didn’t disclose its actions to the FDA, noting that it, too, had been in the dark about this.

Still, Amgen pointed out, none of the underlying data were actually changed, and the reassessment of the data, Amgen maintains, was “conducted to correct a small number of errors.” ChemoCentryx was not legally required to disclose the fact that it revisited the data to the FDA, Amgen maintains.

In an emailed response to questions from Undark that Alison Chartan, director of Amgen’s global media relations team, requested be attributed to a company spokesperson, Amgen reiterated many of the points made in the document submitted to the FDA. “As stated in our response to CDER,” the email noted, “the 2019 data readjudication conducted by ChemoCentryx followed a prespecified procedure to correctly and consistently apply prespecified trial rules to adjudicated outcomes. No clinical data were altered.” The email also emphasized the real-world impact a withdrawal would have on those currently taking Tavneos. “Preserving treatment options for these patients,” Amgen wrote, “is central to our mission.” (The company plans to present new data on Tavneos at a conference in November.)

The FDA does have the authority to withdraw its approval of a drug, said Patricia Zettler, a law professor at The Ohio State University who formerly served as an attorney for the Department of Health and Human Services. The law requires a stepwise approach. As an opening gambit, the agency must give notice and offer the drug’s manufacturer an opportunity for a public hearing. If the manufacturer can demonstrate a genuine disagreement about the facts, then the hearing may be held. After that, the FDA can withdraw approval of the drug. If Amgen disagrees with the decision, it could sue the agency.

All of this leaves patients and physicians in a potentially protracted state of uncertainty about whether Tavneos actually works.

Amgen says it does. To make its case, the company has pointed to an independent re-adjudication of its pivotal trial, conducted by researchers at the Duke Clinical Research Institute, part of the Duke University School of Medicine. Although the drug still didn’t meet the FDA’s bar of higher one-year remission rates, the study participants who received the drug fared no worse on this measure. The company also pointed to real-world data, meaning data collected via routine medical care, suggesting that Tavneos can indeed reduce steroid use.

Chloe Cusano is among those who would like to see Tavneos retain its approval. She received it while in the hospital and credits it with helping her taper off steroids more rapidly. Roberts, the UCSF epidemiologist, said his team’s registry study found low rates of drug-induced liver injuries among patients in the U.S., a finding he characterized as “incredibly reassuring,” particularly when care is coupled with careful monitoring. It’s important to keep in mind, he said, that the current alternative to Tavneos is “much higher levels” of steroids.

Under the law, Tavneos “really shouldn’t remain on the market,” said Joshua Skydel, a clinical fellow in rheumatology at Yale New Haven Hospital and a researcher at the Yale Collaboration for Regulatory Rigor, Integrity, and Transparency. The FDA has standards for drug approval, including substantial evidence of safety and effectiveness. In this case, the pivotal trial has been called into question, and several of the studies that Amgen has pointed to have yet to be published: “I’d at least like to see them go through peer review,” Skydel said, “before hanging my hat on them.”

Høeg, meanwhile, is skeptical that clinical evidence gathered since Tavneos was approved will do much to support its case. “I suspect real world data, much of which were already available when we requested withdrawal in April, will not meet the FDA’s evidentiary bar for approval,” she wrote. “We do know the data were insufficient for ongoing marketing authorization [in] the EU and UK.”

Skydel additionally noted that at the time of Tavneos’ approval, the FDA requested that additional post-marketing studies be conducted. But Amgen has fallen behind on deadlines for those studies. “This episode really, for me, highlighted the way that drugs are allowed to reach the market with open questions,” Skydel said. “Our capacity to answer those questions is really only as strong as FDA and industry’s collaboration,” he continued, as well as FDA’s willingness to use its authority after a drug has gone on the market.

In its April letter, the FDA argued that the stakes of this debate go beyond patients with one rare disease, stating that withdrawing the drug “is critical to protect the public health and the integrity of the drug approval process.” Absent such a consequence, the agency stated, other companies will have an incentive to act deceptively.

Walter Kraft, who voted to recommend approving the drug based on what he knew at the time, also worries about the potential for knock-on effects. The clinical trial system “is built on a level of trust,” he said. “And when that trust is put into question for a narrow parochial gain, it puts the whole system at risk for other subsequent actors in the space.”

#325. Teenage swimmer breaks two world records in four days

Sixteen-year-old Summer McIntosh broke the world record for the 400m individual medley at the Canadian swimming trials on Saturday – just days after breaking the world record for the 400m freestyle.

McIntosh finished the 400m individual medley in a time of 4:25.87, breaking the mark set at the 2016 Rio Olympics by Hungarian swimmer Katinka Hosszú with a time of 4:26.36.

The result continues the teenager’s brilliant week after she broke the 400m freestyle world record last Tuesday – breaking defending Olympic champion Ariarne Titmus’ previous record of 3:56.40, which was set last May, in a time of 3:56.08.

Speaking after her latest triumph, McIntosh shared her emotions.

“That’s the first time I really vividly heard the crowd during my race,” McIntosh said, per Reuters.

“It’s amazing to have all my family and friends in the stands, cheering me on. It really helped me in the last 100 meters.”

The Canadian teen made her Olympic debut aged 14 at Tokyo 2020, where she finished fourth in the 200-meter freestyle.

She bagged gold in the 200m butterfly and 400m medley at the world championships in 2022, as well as two golds at the Commonwealth Games in the 200m and 400m medleys.

She now trains in Florida under coach Brent Arckey with the Sarasota Sharks team.

#324. The best Kindle and e-reader accessories for your coziest reading nook yet

Kindles are the darling device of BookTok, where you can scroll through thousands of videos on the best accessories and gadgets to maximize your reading experience. One thing about the BookTok girlies: They're right. While I've spent hours watching videos of people decking out their Kindles with accessories, I never really understood the extras until I tried them for myself.

Kindle accessories are add-ons like remote page turners, gooseneck stands, clear cases, PopSockets, and hand straps, which are all aimed at improving your reading comfort. These accessories are so popular that even Amazon launched two of its own new accessories in 2026.

You may roll your eyes at a gooseneck stand or page-turning remote — I once did — but you're missing out on a life of luxury. A life that includes a Kindle on a stand, a remote page turner in hand, and you all tucked into the covers.

And keep in mind that while Kindles are the buzziest e-readers, there's a whole lot of love for Kobo e-readers on BookTok and here at Mashable. Even though the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is our favorite e-reader, we still have a lot of love for the Kobo Clara Colour and Kobo Libra Colour.

So if you own a Kindle or use another e-reader, this guide is for you: It features the essential accessories, including stands, remotes, grips, and cases. Plus, all the recently launched remotes from Kobo and Boox.

Remote page turners rose in popularity on BookTok, so much so that Amazon finally launched its own, the Kindle Click, which is compatible with 2024 Kindles or newer.

At the end of the night, when you want to be cozy in bed, tucked under the blanket to stay warm, the remote allows you to do just that. Combined with the gooseneck stand? Nighttime reading is about to be the coziest it's ever been.

And while the page turner is great for getting cozy, it's also ideal for when you're using a Kindle while on the treadmill.

Amazon now makes the Kindle Click, joining the likes of Kobo, Boox, and Durobo. While the Boox Tappy and Durobo Moodi aren't my favorite, the Kobo remote is perfectly designed.

While we expected a Kindle remote to join Amazon's latest batch of Kindles, the more surprising accessory is the new Page Turn Cover. It works seamlessly with Kindles, attaching via magnetic Pogo pins. Once connected, you can use the buttons on the case to turn the page.

It works like a charm, but there's a big catch. The Page Turn Cover only works with the Paperwhite Signature Edition and Colorsoft Signature Edition e-readers, meaning to use the case, you need to have one of those e-readers. Not to mention, the case costs $79.99.

That being said, I love the Page Turn Cover and think it's a worthy investment.

While the remote page turner helps you click through your book, to go truly hands-free, you need to prop up your e-reader, too. Enter the gooseneck stand. After seeing this viral video, I, and the rest of the internet, was influenced to get a clip-in stand for an e-reader.

And let me tell you, it is a luxury to have this stand. While a Kindle is still lightweight, when you're on a reading marathon, your arm inevitably gets tired from holding up the device. But having a gooseneck stand positions the Kindle within reading distance without any arm fatigue.

To test out a gooseneck stand, I tried the Magipea Gooseneck Stand, which is compatible with either a Kindle or Kobo e-reader (I use it with both). I find the bendy arm of this stand to be a little too stiff, but overall, it still works well.

There are plenty of Kindle cases in the sea, but the most popular option among BookTok is a simple, clear case. Sure, that seems boring, but the exciting part is decorating it. Add-ons like charms also bring personal flair, and some people even buy inserts or stickers to swap out over time.

And if you're interested in using a PopSockets grip with your Kindle, I recommend getting a case that's MagSafe compliant so you can take it on and off. PopSockets has its own Kindle case that also happens to be MagSafe.

PopSockets are already the best ergonomic grip for your phone, so why wouldn't they be the best grip for another handheld device? When I'm not using my Kindle with the gooseneck stand, I like using it with a PopSockets grip for an ergonomic hold.

With a traditional PopSockets grip, you attach it to a device with adhesive, but that means once it's on, it's on. But using a MagSafe PopSockets grip allows you to attach and reattach the grip, depending on whether you want your Kindle to lie flat.

I personally use the PopSockets MagSafe Kick-Out Stand with my Kindle since that's what I use on my phone, and I like that I can prop it up to stand vertically. However, PopSockets launched a line of bookish MagSafe grips to go with its line of Kindle cases.

If PopSockets grips aren't really your thing, then Strapsicle makes a nice alternative. Strapsicle's straps attach to the corners of your e-reader, creating a cross pattern. Your hand then slips through the straps, delivering an easy hold on your e-reader. While I personally prefer the feel of a PopSockets grip, the Strapsicle lets your hand lie flat, so it doesn't cramp up from being in a hold. The Strapsicle works best when it has a snug fit, so using it with a case can be a little tight.

Before I went deep into the world of Kindle accessories, I really just wanted a good case. After several well-placed Instagram ads, I landed on a case from Page. Not only do they have a ton of really cute designs, but they also make cases for a variety of e-readers, including the full Kindle and Kobo lineups.

The case automatically wakes and sleeps your e-reader, and it includes a hand strap for a nice grip while reading. Plus, I like this case because it guards the poorly placed power button on the e-reader. This way, when I'm reading on the treadmill, the button doesn't accidentally get pressed.

You could also always go for an official Amazon case for a simple cover with good protection. Any protective case is a good choice, especially one with reinforced corners to protect against drops.

Samantha Mangino, is an e-reader expert. She's tested all the Kindle and Kobo e-readers, diving into the buzziest models. Her love of reading extends beyond the e-reader beat, covering books and authors, too. In the tech space, she covers tablets, smart rings, and headphones.

#323. Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged

A long flight home from feeding grounds messes with birds’ internal clocks.

Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling where the body insists it’s the middle of the night while the clock says it’s lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans.

A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass.

Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales.

From there, they head out to feed anywhere from a few dozen to more than 1,000 kilometers into the Atlantic. To get back, shearwaters are thought to work out where they are located using a map sense, possibly based on smells, and then use the Sun as a compass to set their direction.

The trouble with navigating by the Sun, though, is that it moves across the sky. “You can imagine an animal or a human that wants to travel south all day. At sunrise, when the Sun’s in the east, it needs to be traveling 90 degrees clockwise of the Sun, but by midday it needs to be traveling straight towards the Sun, and by sunset it needs to be traveling 90 degrees anticlockwise of the Sun,” Lewin said. Effective navigation by the Sun requires a clock that tells you what time of day it is. Birds, like nearly all animals, have such a clock built in. But the clock in Manx shearwaters is not perfect.

The birds recalibrate their internal clock at every dusk and dawn. This means that for every degree of longitude a bird covers between sunrise and sunset, its clock falls four minutes out of sync with local time. In consequence, a Manx shearwater misjudges where the Sun should be and veers off course clockwise when it flies east, or anticlockwise when it flies west.

Scientists had already shown something similar in other birds by catching penguins and quickly moving them across lines of longitude, but before Lewin’s study no one had clearly demonstrated it in wild animals moving on their own, mostly because the effect is small and so requires a lot of data to become apparent. But Lewin’s team happened to have just the right database.

Tim Guilford, Lewin’s supervisor at Oxford, and Chris Perrins, a long-time Oxford shearwater researcher, started fitting shearwaters with GPS tags in 2004, when the devices first became small enough for a bird this size. Two decades later, the team had tracks from 3,688 foraging trips made by 1,045 birds from colonies along the UK’s western coasts. Those trips last from one day to up to two weeks.

From this dataset, Lewin and his colleagues separated homeward flights, which the scientists say was rather simple. Foraging shearwaters make short, wiggly flights between dives. “When they are deciding to go back to their colony, they kind of switch into this mode where they are flying as fast as they can in pretty much a straight line continuously without stopping for really long periods,” Lewin said.

For each homing flight, the researchers worked out where the bird last saw the sunrise, at which point its clock should have matched local time. Then, at every GPS fix, they calculated how far east or west it had traveled since, and how much that would bend its Sun compass. Since they knew each bird was headed exactly to its burrow, they could compare those predictions with how the birds actually deviated from their course.

The time shifts were tiny. “About an hour is pretty much the maximum that we observed. Most of these are probably 15-minute, 10-minute time differences,” Lewin says. “For us, that would be pretty imperceptible, but it does still have an effect on their compass orientation that we can detect.”

Across 335 homing flights made out of sight of land, the birds veered just as the Sun compass predictions said they would. Because the study was not a controlled experiment, though, Lewin argues we need to be careful about causality. Still, the team calculated the biases that crosswinds, the Coriolis effect, or a magnetic compass might introduce, and none of those fit the data well. “Our observed biases match by far the best to the Sun compass biases that we would expect,” Lewin said.

The navigational errors apparently caused by jet lag reached up to around 15 degrees, which for birds was way less costly than one might expect. A bird with a map sense can check its position, notice it’s drifting, and correct. The team calculated that for a shearwater flying 1,000 kilometers east in a day, about the maximum the scientists observed, the average error would be roughly 7 degrees. If the bird keeps checking where it is, that adds only 5 kilometers to the trip.

The researchers also found that when shearwaters followed coastlines, they still drifted slightly closer to or farther from the shore depending on their expected compass error. Work done in Oxford two decades ago showed that homing pigeons with shifted clocks do the same, even while following a familiar road. This led researchers to hypothesize that birds may run two parallel navigation systems, one based on the compass and one on familiar landmarks, with the balance between them never tipping entirely to one side.

An alternative explanation, Lewin suggests, might be that they don’t know exactly where on the coast they are and use the Sun to pick which way to follow it. “We don’t quite know. And I think it’s an interesting question, especially as people try and design bio-inspired autonomous navigation systems,” Lewin says.

Lewin’s study could not answer whether Manx shearwaters suffer from other jet lag symptoms, like poor sleep or hunger at odd hours. “We’ve not been able to investigate that yet,” Lewin said. The next step for his team would be finding out whether the time shifts affect when birds forage, how much food they bring home, and their breeding success. Another question is whether more animals routinely experience jet lag. Lewin thinks it’s quite likely.

The same jet lag effect, Lewin said, could hit any organism with an internal clock that moves far enough east or west in a single day. That mostly means fliers, or animals living near the poles, where lines of longitude are packed closer together. The long-term goal is to find out whether animals that constantly suffer from jet lag evolved some ways to cope with it.

“In humans, if you do it a lot, in the long term it has really negative health impacts,” Lewin said. “So maybe we could take some inspiration from these animals that are constantly experiencing jet lag and see if there are ways that we can mitigate jet lag affecting humans.”

Science, 2026.  DOI: 10.1126/science.adz2542

#322. Angel Reese defends gesture directed towards Caitlin Clark after LSU national title win; calls out double standard after being 'unapologetically' her

LSU star Angel Reese defended the gesture she aimed at Iowa Hawkeyes’ Caitlin Clark near the end of the Tigers’ first NCAA women’s basketball national championship victory on Sunday, saying “I don’t take disrespect lightly.”

Reese could be seen approaching Clark before moving her open hand in front of her face – popularized by WWE star John Cena to mean “you can’t see me” – before pointing to her ring finger in a gesture some interpreted as a reference to the place her newly-acquired championship ring might sit.

Caitlin Clark breaks records galore during historic March Madness run

Clark made a similar gesture to another player earlier in the tournament.

The gesture has sparked much debate, especially on social media. Some have criticized Reese, while others have defended her actions, highlighting how there was no public outrage in response to Clark’s gesture earlier in the tournament.

Sports journalist Jose de Jesus Ortiz called Reese’s actions “classless,” while former ESPN host Keith Olbermann called Reese an “idiot” for the gesture.

In the press conference after the victory, Reese referenced the difference in reaction she received as a result of her gesture as compared to the one Clark received.

“All year, I was critiqued for who I was. I don’t fit the narrative,” Reese said. “I don’t fit the box that y’all want me to be in. I’m too hood. I’m too ghetto. Y’all told me that all year. But when other people do it, and y’all don’t say nothing.

“So this is for the girls that look like me. For those that want to speak up for what they believe in. It’s unapologetically you. And that’s what I did it for tonight. It was bigger than me tonight. And Twitter is going to go into a rage every time.

“And I’m happy. I feel like I’ve helped grow women’s basketball this year. (…) I’m looking forward to celebrating and then next season.”

LSU beats Iowa to win its first NCAA women's basketball championship

Reese had 15 points and 10 rebounds in the 102-85 victory and won the women’s March Madness’ Most Outstanding Player award.

In the post-game broadcast, Reese referenced the similar gesture Clark made to a Louisville opponent in the Elite Eight.

In the same game, Clark said to an opponent: “You’re down by 15 points. Shut up,” according to the Bleacher Report.

“Caitlin Clark is a hell of a player but I don’t take disrespect lightly,” Reese said. “She disrespected [LSU’s] Alexis [Morris] (…) and I wanted to pick her pocket. But I had a moment at the end of her game. I was in my bag, I was in my moment.”

After the Championship game, Clark herself said she didn’t notice anything at the time.

“I was just trying to get to the handshake line and shake hands and be grateful that my team was in that position,” Clark said in the post-game press conference. “All the credit in the world to LSU. They were tremendous. They deserve it. They had a tremendous season.

“(LSU head coach) Kim Mulkey coached them so, so well. She’s one of the best basketball coaches of all time, and it shows. She only said really kind things to me in the handshake line, so I’m very grateful of that too.

“But honestly I have no idea. I was just trying to spend the last few moments on the court with especially the five people that I’ve started 93 games with and relishing every second of that.”

LSU head coach Mulkey said she had “no clue” about what transpired.

Among those defending Reese on social media were ESPN’s Holly Rowe and former NBA star Etan Thomas.

“People hating on Angel Reese or Caitlin Clark. Stop. Unapologetically confident young women should be celebrated NOT hated. Get used to it,” Rowe wrote on Twitter.

Former Washington Wizards, Oklahoma City Thunder and Atlanta Hawks player Thomas wrote: “Hold on now!!!! It was cute when Caitlin Clark did it. Y’all didn’t have any issues with it at all. So don’t be all outraged and talking about class and sportsmanship when Angel Reese does the same thing. We’re not doing double standards here.”

Reese said the negative reaction on social media throughout the season has helped fuel her excellent season, having finished averaging 23.0 points and 15.4 rebounds in her first season with LSU after transferring from Maryland.

“Twitter can say what they want to say,” she said. “I love reading those comments. I have all the screenshots of what everybody has said about me all season. What are you going to say now?”

#321. What to do if your smart home devices keep disconnecting from Wi-Fi

It's strange that Apple is only now beginning to take the smart home market seriously with the launch of the HomeView smart display and the rest of the Apple Home Collection. Affordable consumer gear has been around for years, and when it's well-made and well-configured, it can not only simplify your life but also save you money. Smart thermostats are more efficient, and smart lighting can be set to turn on only when and where you need it — although it's more fun to make your living room look like Los Angeles in Blade Runner 2049.

One hassle is that some accessories don't play well with Wi-Fi. They have a tendency to drop out of apps, assuming you can even set them up in the first place. And needless to say, a home fixture you can't count on is all but worthless. You wouldn't put up with a microwave that only cooked dinner on Tuesdays and Fridays.

Thankfully, there are a few tactics you can use to cope with these misbehaving devices. We're not going to lie, though — in some circumstances, a hardware upgrade is in order. You may want to minimize the number of Wi-Fi-based products in your home in general.

If you're still using a Wi-Fi 5 router, stop everything and upgrade to Wi-Fi 6 or 7. The issue is connection limits. On Wi-Fi 5, the practical limit for simultaneous connections is around 10 to 25 devices, perhaps 30 if you're lucky. That's plenty in a home without smart home gear, but once accessories start filling up those connection slots, problems are inevitable. Your router is going to start kicking some devices to make room, and chances are your phone and laptop are going to win out over a lamp.

Another problem is that many cheaper accessories are limited to the 2.4GHz band. On a mesh Wi-Fi system, setting up these accessories can be difficult or impossible, since there's a unified SSID (network ID) with automatic band steering — your phone might end up on 5 or 6GHz, preventing some apps from detecting the new gear. If you're lucky enough to successfully configure a product, there might still be a possibility of later detection failures.

Speaking of which, let's talk about HomeKit. Apple's platform is prone to "No Response" errors in situations where Amazon Alexa and Google Home operate just fine. The company has tried to smooth this out in recent years with an overhauled framework, but if you want a bulletproof setup, you may need an equally bulletproof Wi-Fi network. That could include two or more Apple home hubs for the sake of control redundancy. You can use a mix of HomePods, HomeViews or Apple TV 4Ks.

There's also a more basic concern we haven't touched on yet, and that's range. If an accessory is sitting on the fringes, it's naturally going to drop out when conditions are less than ideal. If you can't reposition devices or your router, it may be time to upgrade to a mesh system, as long as that doesn't wreak havoc for specific accessories. Alternatively, if you have a standalone router, you might try enabling separate 2.4 and 5GHz SSIDs, and forcing all of your smart home accessories over to the longer-range 2.4GHz band.

Ultimately, the best approach is to transition as many accessories as possible over to alternate protocols, namely Thread, Zigbee or Z-Wave. These do require a Wi-Fi hub, or in the case of Thread, a Wi-Fi-enabled "border router" accessory. The benefit, however, is that they not only reduce the burden on your Wi-Fi network but they also tend to be faster and more reliable. They're mesh-based — extending their reach — and hub-based accessories (like Philips Hue Zigbee lights) can continue to run some automations when the internet is down.

Thread is probably your best bet, since some routers, speakers and displays have border router features built in, as do products like Nanoleaf light panels. There is an asterisk, though: bandwidth. Like Zigbee and Z-Wave, Thread is a low-power standard, so it simply can't carry enough data for functions like audio, video or even vacuuming. It's mostly limited to bulbs, locks, plugs and sensors.

Some degree of Wi-Fi reliance is unavoidable, then. But if you find the right mix and know how to troubleshoot recurring issues, it shouldn't be a big deal. Just have fallbacks ready for internet outages.

#320. The 8 best headphones of 2026: We tested the top contenders from Sony, Apple, Bose, and Beats

In 2026, a pair of headphones or earbuds is pretty much non-optional. That's why there are hundreds of different headphones shapes, sizes, styles, colors, and, of course, prices. These days, you can grab a random pair off the digital shelf without too much research and find that they do the job just fine. However, if you're tired of settling for "just fine," then it's worth investing in the best headphones available.

But be warned: The latest generation of flagship noise-cancelling headphones from the likes of Apple, Sony, and Bose will set you back $450 or more, though we have options to recommend for every price range.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

To help you find the best pair of headphones possible, our experts test headphones year-round, from popular models to new releases to budget picks (you can learn more about our detailed testing standards below). The result of that vetting is this guide, which we keep updated regularly to give you the most accurate and current purchasing information possible. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Read our full review of the Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones.

Audiophiles and custom equalizer fans: After three years, Sony's flagship wireless headphones finally got an update. If you love Sony headphones and have an old pair of XM4s, then we can definitely recommend an upgrade. However, if you just purchased a pair of XM5s, then it might be harder to justify an instant upgrade. That said, the active noise cancellation is better than ever, and there are noticeable improvements to audio quality (even if they lose out by a smidge to the latest Technics AZ100 earbuds). Besides music lovers, travelers will also appreciate the new Sony cans, as they fold up and come with an improved travel case.

Mashable's Tech Editor Timothy Beck Werth reviewed the XM6 headphones ahead of their launch, and he was impressed with the overall quality. As Werth wrote in his review, "The new Sony headphones offer impressive audio quality, and they definitely improve on the XM5 models. The active noise cancellation is particularly phenomenal...I really appreciated the overall balance, depth, and quality of the audio. For the XM6, Sony audio engineers worked with music mastering engineers here in the United States, and the results are clear when you listen to music. Like all headphone reviewers, I have a dedicated playlist for testing new audio products, and I found that vocal-heavy tracks sound particularly great, with noticeable improvements over the XM5s."

Sony introduced (or, rather, brought back) a major design change for the XM6 headphones — they fold up for easier storage. They're definitely more compact and easier to travel with compared to the previous-gen model. The overall design looks similar, so if you're a fan of the Sony aesthetic, you'll still appreciate how they look.

We do wish there had been slightly bigger improvements after a three-year wait, and the battery life (30 hours with ANC engaged) is the same as the XM5 model, which we also loved. These headphones did arrive with a higher sticker price, so if you can't quite swing the $448 price tag, look for the excellent XM5 headphones on sale.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones (2nd gen).

Those who want the best of the best: For anyone who's yet to buy into the Bose QuietComfort Ultra line, but wants noise-cancelling headphones that can easily handle long hours of wear, there's no better choice than the second generation Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones.

The best noise-cancelling headphones aren't much use if they squeeze your head too tight or prevent you from wearing accessories like earrings or glasses comfortably. In other words, comfort is key — we were big fans of Bose's first gen QC Ultra headphones for exactly this reason.

With the second generation of the headphones, Bose makes minor improvements to the soundscape, noise-cancelling, and somehow the wear. They also fixed other bugs that detracted from the otherwise premium experience of using the QC Ultras.

As a first step, Bose upped the battery life from 24 to 30 hours per charge with ANC. They also added options for wired playback with the USB-C cable (which can simultaneously charge the headphones) or the auxiliary cable for passive playback (which wasn't available on the first gen headphones). In tandem with the battery life, these headphones become much stronger contenders for travel.

For day-to-day use, Bose's noise cancelling remains as solid as ever (though Sony's XM6s are ever so slightly more adept at handling high pitched frequencies), while offering an easy adjustment on 10 different levels of ANC via the companion app. As for the listening experience, the immersive audio remains as lackluster as it did on the first gen, but the overall sound profile came through richer and more robust when we compared the headphones side by side. Bose also added quality of life adjustments like better wear detection, and a lay flat mode that puts the headphones into a low power mode when they're placed face down. Overall, it's hard to beat this blend of sound quality, ANC, and comfort, making the second iteration of the QC Ultras one of our top picks for headphones.

Value fiends: If you don't particularly care to have the most premium pair of headphones on the market (or care to spend several hundred dollars on them), the JLab JBuds Lux ANC headphones are the best budget headphones available. They have functional ANC, decent comfort, great sound balance, and a killer battery life, all with a design that doesn't feel cheap.

At their regular sale price of around $50, these are about a ninth the price of the latest Sony headphones, and a seventh of the price of the Bose QuietComfort headphones, which feel like these headphones' premium analogue.

With budget headphones, it's good to understand what you're trading off from the jump. In the case of these JLab headphones, the ANC will dampen a good amount of environmental sound, from talking coworkers to loud fans, but it won't completely silence the world around you. The app can lag some (we had to exit out of it a few times during testing when it froze), and the fit of these headphones might not be for everyone. For one of our testers, these headphones squeezed their head more than usual (though some users on Reddit called these the most comfortable headphones they've tried). Regardless of the fit, you're likely to hear some creaking from time to time when you move your head around.

At $80, these are all cons that may not be ideal, but are fair for the price point. At these headphones' frequent sale prices that hover in the $50 to $55 range, these cons are even easier to swallow, especially when you consider how these headphones actually sound.

To be clear, you'll likely need to play around with the EQ some to find your perfect settings — we found the first preset to be on the bass-heavy end. Once you do, it's impressive the way these headphones can balance a song. Every part of Panic! At The Disco's "Northern Downpour" shone through, from the vocals, lead guitar, bass, and piano. For budget headphones, we might expect some muddying through these elements, but the JLab JBuds held up great. If we're being nitpicky, The Beatles' "In My Life" came through somewhat dimmer sounding than expected, but not necessarily muddy.

Beyond the sound signature, these headphones have a reasonable amount of customization with the app, especially for their price point. You can adjust the button commands on one of the three on-ear buttons, adjust the ANC intensity with a slider in the app, and create your own custom EQ settings. Multipoint pairing is available, as are spatial audio, music, and movie modes.

Check out our full guide to the best Sony headphones.

Students, casual users, and anyone looking for great sound on the cheap: The new price of entry for flagship noise-cancelling headphones? A cool $450, at least. So, if you're looking for wireless headphones with true active noise cancellation but don't want to spend more than $100, then go with Sony's mid-range noise-cancellers. They have Sony's signature sound (and signature all-plastic design, sadly), and you can almost always find them on sale for under $100 at Amazon and other retailers.

These headphones perform much better than you'd expect a pair of $100 cans to perform. They have surprisingly impressive ANC and multipoint pairing, as well as impressive sound — hardly a surprise with a pair of Sony headphones.

As our reviewer Alex Bracetti wrote, "The WH-CH720 employs 30mm drivers and exclusive brand technologies to broaden sound performance. Expect a vibrant mix of impactful bass with striking mids and highs. Turning on DSEE raises fidelity on poor-quality recordings, which many luxury headphones can’t do. You can tweak the sound to your liking via the EQ, though the headphones sound great on their default setting."

Read our full review of the Nothing Headphone (a).

Folks too busy to charge their devices: If you're just a little too familiar with the low battery sound on your headphones, the absurdly long battery life on the Nothing Headphone (a) gets you as close as you can to a guarantee that you'll hear it as little as possible. Plus, it has a standout retro design.

Picking the headphones with the best battery life isn't a terribly complex process. That said, it isn't just about picking the pair that can pack the most hours — it's about finding the headphones with the best combination of value, overall performance, and, of course, battery life.

Our standard before was set at 60 hours, which is a great deal higher than the 30 hours you'll find on the Bose and Sony headphones on this list. The Nothing Headphone (a) absolutely blows that standard out of the water, offering 75 hours per charge with ANC on, and 135 hours without.

They check the remaining boxes at $199, which, while not dirt cheap, is a fair deal cheaper than most $400+ flagship models. The sound quality is clear and robust, the noise cancellation will get the job done (if not flawlessly), and the on-ear controls are truly a thing of perfection. During testing, we almost never reached for our devices when adjusting settings because the on-ear controls made it so easy not to. Rounding out the experience is a companion app that's easy to navigate, with features like an eight-band equalizer designed to make your music sound just to your liking.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort headphones (2nd gen).

Travelers, students, and anyone blending comfort and value: A lot about our most comfortable headphones pick sounds great, but you're caught up on the price point — understandable. Though a truly excellent, well-rounded headphones experience often comes with a higher price point, Bose's latest headphones — the second generation QuietComforts — prove that investment doesn't need to exceed $400 (for now).

If you're looking for extreme comfort, quality ANC, warm and balanced sound, and a few extras without totally breaking the bank, these are your headphones.

These aren't perfect headphones. The sound profile isn't the most customizable with a three-band equalizer, there's no truly passive playback with the wired connections, the noise cancellation will get staticky during a plane takeoff, and the battery life leans on the low side at 24 hours (finding 30 hours or up isn't too hard these days on a pair of over-ear headphones).

All this to say, these aren't technically perfect headphones, but those cons pale in comparison to their pros. At $359, these headphones are nearly $100 cheaper than the Bose QC Ultra 2 headphones, but offer many of the same features. For starters, the comfort and noise cancellation are nearly on par with the significantly more expensive headphones, which is to say it's very, very good — like easily wearable for a full day of travel. The tactile controls are intuitive and functional, the colorways are varied and unique while remaining appealing, and there's an Immersive Audio listening mode for changing up how you hear your music.

In a time when most tech prices are rising, it's refreshing to see a brand release a pair of headphones that strive for ultra-premium performance, while sticking to a more mildly premium price point.

Read our original review of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones, or see how they compare to the new XM6 headphones.

Last-gen lovers: If you want a premium pair of Sony noise-cancelling headphones but refuse to pay more than $400 for a pair of headphones, we feel you. We also have good news: The XM5 headphones hold up well in 2026, and they're still worth the investment, especially when they're on sale.

Originally released in 2022, the Sony XM5 headphones are still legendary. They had unbeatable ANC and sound for the money, and even in 2026, they sound shockingly good. That's because the new flagship XM6 model only made iterative improvements over these cans. So, now that they go on sale for as little as $248, you just can't write off the older XM5s.

This Mashable Choice product received a 4.7 out of 5 stars in our original review, and even when we recently compared them head-to-head with their successors, they performed incredibly well.

We won't beat around the bush: There's no definitive "best" product here. Sure, elite audio brands put out high-quality products across the board, but even within each of those brands, you'll find different tiers of products. Some will deliver better value, and some will deliver better hardware and active noise cancellation.

All this to say, the best pair of earbuds or headphones largely comes down to personal preference and how you plan to use them. Some listeners swear by over-ear headphones, while others prefer the minimalism of earbuds — one is not necessarily better than the other. Athletes who like to use headphones at the gym will appreciate waterproof materials and the best open earbuds, while frequent fliers will prefer devices with long battery life, comfort, and portability. Finally, music lovers and audiophiles will want to invest in premium features like a custom equalizer, spatial audio, or best-in-class active noise cancellation.

To help you pick your pair, we tested all of the headphones in this guide (and a lot that didn't make the cut). Here, you'll find the top headphones of 2026 for noise cancellation, music, price, and wired connections.

We focused primarily on the best wireless headphones for this guide. While wired headphones have their fans, wireless headphones are just more convenient for most of us, though some of us are also fans of Apple's EarPods. With the release of the new noise-cancelling wired earbuds from Bose, we will be keeping our testing pool open to more wired models and will update this guide accordingly, should any earn a spot.

Most recently, we tested the Marshall Monitor III, JBL Tour One M3 headphones, and the Skullcandy Method 360 ANC, and though they had their merits, they fell short of winning the best of the best spot on this guide.

We've also tested the Sonos Ace headphones and Dyson OnTrac headphones. And while we loved them both for sound quality and noise cancellation, they fare in the way of AirPods Max — left out of our recommendations for their high price points.

We'll be comparing them against our current picks to see if they have a spot among our favorites.

No, we didn't forget to include the iconic Apple AirPods Max in our guide to the best headphones. It's not that we don't like them — in fact, we think they sound and look great (emphasis on look). However, after testing and re-testing them, we think they're just too expensive to justify a wholehearted recommendation. While we appreciate that they now (finally) come with lossless audio, they're still behind on features like battery life.

While they're still a smart choice for style-conscious Apple fans, we can no longer include them among the elite. We thought they were way too expensive upon their initial release, and we only feel more firm in this position six years later.

While the long-anticipated AirPods Max 2 are finally out, our reviewer found the upgrades to be minimal. At the same $549 the original Maxes were released at, these headphones are just too expensive and underperforming for us to recommend them.

Like with most products, this comes down to personal preference, but there are a few brands known for making really solid headphones. For those who appreciate quality ANC above all else, Bose headphones will be the best brand. Enjoy a rich and balanced sound profile? You'll want to check out Sony. In the budget space, Anker Soundcore products have impressed us lately. Still, we recommend reading each of our above picks to see which speaks most to you.

If you're wondering what headphones you've been seeing all over your For You page, it's likely a pair of Sonys, either the older WH-1000XM5s or the brand new Sony WH-1000XM6s. The former two used to be our top picks, but the XM6s now take the crown. Beats headphones are also incredibly popular, especially as brands like Marshall and Jabra fall out of favor.

Other than those, the Bose QuietComfort line is a popular pick, especially for those who wear their headphones for long periods of time. And of course, Apple AirPods are a popular pick for iPhone users who prefer earbuds over headphones. We're not huge fans of the AirPods Max, though, as we think they're too overpriced for what they offer. However, with Apple's recent updates to the AirPods line, we know they are top of mind.

Every single pair of headphones we included in this guide was hands-on tested by a Mashable reporter, editor, or contributor. You can learn about our in-depth process by taking a look at the standardized testing guide we developed for this category.

Below, you'll find our condensed testing criteria for headphones:

We listened to a wide variety of genres of music, podcasts, and other forms of media. If a pair didn't at least sound solid across the board, they didn't make our list. In this category, we also considered the quality (and existence) of any equalizers.

We'll test ANC power around our homes as we work, with and without an audio assist, and outdoors. If headphones have customizable ANC levels, or automatic switching between noise-cancelling modes, we make sure that they actually provide noticeable differences in performance.

Everything from comfort to touch controls fall under this category. We look at what headphones offer to provide the best wear for the greatest amount of people, whether that be a strong selection of earbud tip sizes or particularly soft padding. Whenever possible, we test and re-test headphones over longer periods of time to see how they hold up.

We evaluate how headphones perform in all of the above categories, and if that performance matches their price point.
